questions.problem: If ${f}^{′}(x)=|x-1|$ and $f(2)=3,$ which of the following could be the graph of a continuous function  $y=f(x)?$
questions.worked_solution:
The graph of $y={f}^{′}(x)$ is the following:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14273358/assets/270130d95065a37b075cb070da220bb774dc56bf096937cdba3755b3858615a1.png)

Recall that critical points of $y=f(x)$ occur when ${f}^{′}(x)=0$ or ${f}^{′}(x)$ does not exist. In our case, there is one critical point: 

$\,$ $x=1$ 

Also, we have the following: 

- If ${f}^{′}(x)>0$ then $f(x)$ is increasing.

- If ${f}^{′}(x)<0$ then $f(x)$ is decreasing.

We can now summarize the information from the graph in the table below.

| $x$ | $(-\infty ,1)$ | $1$ | $(1,\infty )$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ${f}^{′}$ | $+$ | $0$ | $+$ |
| $f$ | $↗$ | $\text{no extr.}$ | $↗$ |

Let's now sketch the graph of $y=f(x):$

- First, we draw the critical point. Consider the vertical line $x=1.$

- Since we are told that $f(2)=3,$ we can draw that point on the graph.

- Since $f(x)$ is increasing $↗$ on $(1,2),$ the point at $x=1$ must be lower than the point at $x=2.$

So, we draw it as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14273358/assets/995f590bbe6017ed49a4f62dad869c868343c1aa3f4aae026b636abb70e7246e.png)

- Next, we consider the behavior of $y=f(x)$ in the neighborhood of the critical points:

- Since $f(x)$ is increasing $↗$ on $(-\infty ,1)$ and is increasing $↗$ on $(1,\infty )$, the graph of $y=f(x)$ goes down to the left of $x=1$ and goes up to the right of $x=1.$

- Furthermore, since ${f}^{′}(x)$ is decreasing to the left of $x=1$, we must have ${f}^{″}(x)<0$, and, since it is increasing to the right of $x=1$, we must have ${f}^{″}(x)>0.$ So, $x=1$ is an inflection point at which the curve $y=f(x)$ changes from concave down to concave up.

So, we can draw as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14273358/assets/f46b93b49d78fe2d7f5ee2dee238abab1cb3fbd1d505bca3bb2e903b3e770d92.png)

- Finally, since we are told that our graph must be continuous, by connecting and extending the existing parts with a smooth curve, we obtain a possible graph of $y=f(x):$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14273358/assets/0bc495bddd2a2082f17cd414f3e75c3c2a76b1fb934f7adecdc78f515b64efe2.png)

The graph of $y={f}^{′}(x),$ the derivative of $f(x),$ is shown above. Which of the following could be the graph of $y=f(x)?$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that critical points of $y=f(x)$ occur when ${f}^{′}(x)=0$ or ${f}^{′}(x)$ does not exist. In our case, there are two critical points: 

$\,$ $x=-2\,$ and $\,x=2$

Also, we have the following: 

- If ${f}^{′}(x)>0$ then $f(x)$ is increasing.

- If ${f}^{′}(x)<0$ then $f(x)$ is decreasing.

We can now summarize the information from the graph in the table below.

| $x$ | $(-\infty ,-2)$ | $-2$ | $(-2,2)$ | $2$ | $(2,\infty )$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ${f}^{′}$ | $+$ | $0$ | $-$ | $0$ | $+$ |
| $f$ | $↗$ | $\text{max}$ | $↘$ | $\text{min}$ | $↗$ |

Let's now sketch the graph of $y=f(x):$

- First, we draw the critical points. We choose an arbitrary point on the vertical lines $x=-2$ and $x=2.$ Since $f(x)$ is decreasing $↘$ on $(-2,2),$ the point at $x=-2$ must be higher than the point at $x=2,$ as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14273358/assets/b6cd3262457eefb38eb0f82339f5f8217d25bc523ecc3fc926b8eee7d3e1fa76.png)

- Next, we consider the behavior of $y=f(x)$ in the neighborhood of the critical points:

- Since $f(x)$ is increasing $↗$ on $(-\infty ,-2)$ and is decreasing $↘$ on $(-2,2)$, the graph of $y=f(x)$ goes down to the left and to the right of $x=-2.$

- Since $f(x)$ is decreasing $↘$ on $(-2,2)$ and is increasing $↗$ on $(2,\infty )$, the graph of $y=f(x)$ goes up to the left and to the right of $x=2.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14273358/assets/6da8fba623c9b26bcfd368079932860242afb04c2b8708980b834b5b837658f3.png)

- Finally, by connecting and extending the existing parts with a smooth curve, we obtain a possible graph of $y=f(x):$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14273358/assets/9547f2867a67a75d3ed9bdf74f62feb5a53c8d869e59f1a8621115fcc8dddb12.png)

 

**Note:** The graph we obtained is not the only possible one. Any similar graph that's shifted vertically up or down could also be considered a possible $y=f(x).$
